GPT-3 was released in 2020 and marked a breakthrough in language modeling. The ability to generate coherent text and answer questions at scale was a major step forward, but GPT-3 had notable shortcomings. It struggled with long-term coherence, would often derail with its own output, and had a hard time with topics it was unfamiliar with.
Larger models like GPT-3 and GPT-4 can answer complex questions and generate long-form explanations, but they also have to be managed carefully. Even small changes to the prompt can lead to wildly different results, with a small number of tokens being the difference between incoherent output, useful output, or harmful output.
Andrej Karpathy has called context engineering “the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step”. In the following series of posts I want to cover the seven components that fill the context window, how they can fail, and give a real token budget.
Part 2 of the series covers RAG in more depth
Part 3 covers memory
Part 4 covers agents
Part 5 covers multi-agent coordination
The components of a context window:
- The system prompt
- The previous model output
- The previous model input
- The next model input
- The next model output
- The next model previous output
- The next model previous input
The system prompt is one of the seven components that fill the context window. When designing a system prompt, you have to carefully choose your words to ensure the model doesn’t go off track.
- Early context windows were only 4, K tokens
- Context windows have grown to 200 K tokens
- The system prompt is the first component of the context window, followed by previous model output and input, then the next model input and output, and so on
- The token budget example comes from a diabetes management coaching agent the author built with LangGraph

In the last post, we talked about retrieving a chunk of text from a ~200,100-token window. Now let's talk about how to use that window to run a query.
The first thing to recognize is that it doesn't work to take the ~200-token query and perform a hard search for the most similar 200-token text in the ~200,100-token window. The window is just too big, and the similarity search would take way too long. You can do a soft-similarity search with some subset of the conversation history, but that will only get you 4-10 candidates, and the quality of those candidates isn't great.
Instead, you have to decompose your query into a set of small rules or queries. Then you can run those rules through the same 200-token input as your decision logic. The rules need to be small because we can't just keep adding context to our queries. The LongMemEval benchmark showed that models given the full ~115,100-token conversation history performed worse than models given only the relevant subset. ~200,100-token conversation history seems to be the ceiling for current frontier models, after which output quality degrades substantially.
The single most important optimization we can do is to organize our rules as a tree, and then perform a depth-first search. This keeps the number of candidate rules roughly proportional to the number of decision rules we're using, rather than the cubic number of rules we would get if we tried to brute-force all the rule combinations. The downside is that we will sometimes have to make some bad decisions because our more nuanced rules were further down the tree and thus not considered. We'll get to the details of how we choose which rules to drop in a future post.
Given this constraint, how do we think about organizing our set of rules?
This is where thinking tokens come in. In the example above, the query isn't for "What are the signs of diabetes?", but rather "The patient has diabetes. How do I care for them?". In the first case, we would return a single rule. In the second case, we have multiple rules we can use to answer the question. The rules are assembled from the patient profile and the concepts in the conversation history. The concepts in the conversation history are, themselves, a product of our rule template and the remaining text in the conversation history. It's turtles all the way down.
Thinking tokens are the cost of the data structures that track the state of the conversation, the knowledge that's in context, and the rules used for reasoning about the conversation. Claude Code has thinking tokens in the form of skills and plugins. In OpenAI's GPT-4, thinking tokens are called "o-series". In OpenAI's GPT-5, the thinking tokens are called "reasoning tokens". Gemini's thinking token unit is called the "thinking budget". In Claude Code's extended thinking, thinking tokens exist in the form of workflow instructions ("debug systematically", "do TDD") and third-party extensions.
In the example above, the thinking token is the patient profile. It's a single concept that we can access in any rule, so it's not a lot of thinking tokens. The rule itself is a separate thinking token. At Manus's scale, where we have dozens of rules, thinking tokens start to dominate.
To give a concrete example, Manus has a tool for cache management that tries to keep the best-performing tools in the cache. When you don't need a rule from a tool, the rule gets evicted from the cache. When you need the rule again, the rule is fetched from the database and put back into the cache. The first time you call the rule, it has to be fetched from the database. The first time, it costs ~200 tokens. On subsequent calls, it costs ~200 tokens. The rule itself is ~200 tokens.
The Manus's solution is logits masking, where the tools stay in context but are suppressed at the decoding level through a state machine. When tools are needed, they're dynamically loaded, processed, and then removed from the cache. Of course, now the rule is ~200 tokens instead of ~200 tokens, so the net cost of the rule is higher.
Manus found that dynamically loading and removing tools breaks their KV-cache. The state block is 50-100 tokens, and you can't get rid of it without performance degrading. Changing the JSON key ordering in a tool definition invalidates the cache from that point forward. Toggling features like web search invalidates the system cache. The net effect is that the thinking tokens cost 10 times more than the uncached token cost.
In our example above, we have two rules. The rule itself is ~200 tokens. The rule is for a value of a single object property. In the rule, we have a condition filter which means that a Type 2 patient never sees Type 1 insulin pump troubleshooting guides, without the patient or model specifying that constraint. In the example, the rule is ~200-300 tokens.
Manus's rule structure requires 200-300 tokens per rule, but Manus has ~70 rules, so the total cost is 10-200 x 200-300 tokens = 40-70,100 tokens. In our example, these rules might generate a list of recommendations for the patient to consider, so the final output token budget might be ~200-300 tokens, meaning we have a 10-200:1 cost difference between cached and uncached tokens.
In the first post, we talked about how the rule template for GPT-300 was 200 tokens, and the rule itself was ~200 tokens. That means a moderately complex schema with nested objects, descriptions, and enums consumes 300+ tokens.
Most frontier models claim support for 1,200,100 tokens or even 2,200,100 tokens. In our case, though, the input-to-output token ratio is about 100:1. That means you can only fit ~200-100 tokens into the conversation history, after which the model starts to perform worse.
Converging on roughly the same set of components
It's surprising how many of the components of context engineering are the same. Manus, Anthropic, and LangChain have converged on roughly the same decomposition of context. The state block is 50-100 tokens. The web search functionality is ~200 tokens. The rule template is ~200 tokens. The rules themselves are ~200-300 tokens. The JSON keys for the KV-cache are 300 tokens. There are separate blocks for each rule. The decision logic has its own block. The conversation history has its own block. At the bottom, the conversation history is limited to ~200,100 tokens. After that, the model's performance drops off.
The only place where there are significant differences is in KV-cache and rule management. Manus's rule management is a state machine, while Anthropic's rule management is through a state block. Anthropic and OpenAI both offer explicit cache control, with up to 90% discounts on cached input tokens. Claude Code has a rule-based structure for keeping the most useful rules in the cache. My rule-based approach is to write rules that are very specific about which objects to create, and then use the rule template to fill in the blanks.
There are also differences in how the rules get to the model. In Claude Code, the rules are loaded into the context window only when the current task calls for them. In LangChain, the rules are loaded at the beginning of the conversation and then stay available throughout the conversation. In my system, I have to break the agent system prompt into XML-tagged sections. Then, each section gets its own rule that is loaded into the context window. The rules are written to the KV-cache, and the rule templates are written to the conversation history.
In terms of the data structures used, all of the systems are using a KV-cache for rule definitions. The Manus system prompt is encoded using a similar structure to the state block, with a fixed number of blocks. The state block reports the current turn, the conversation phase, the time of day and which tools were already called. In my system, I break the agent system prompt into XML-tagged sections, and then each section gets its own rule template that is loaded into the context window. The rules themselves are written to the KV-cache.
The only real differences are in how the data structures are loaded into the conversation history, how the rules are loaded into the conversation history, and how the rules are managed in the context window.
The dream of keeping all of our tools in the conversation history, and then only calling the tools that we need to call, at the moment we need to call them, is a dream for now. The reality is that most of our rules are ~200-300 tokens and our input-to-output token ratio is 100:1. At our scale, with 4-6 tools, not 40, the cost of the tools and the rules dominates. At Manus's scale, with dozens of tools, the cache math probably dominates.
This post has been about how to do retrieval and evaluation in depth, and next post will be about using the conversation history for context.
Update: If you enjoyed reading this post, you might like my book, "Notes from a System's Topic".
Update: New post is out on using the conversation history for context.
Update: LangChain has a great post on their KV-cache and rule management system.

I am using these context engineering strategies to refine the Manus agent. While the agent has been outperforming other agents on the risk charting task, the performance is not that much better than a human agent following standard evidence-based protocols. I want to close the gap!
The manuscript project is a diarized case study, written by a patient and performed with an agent
The Manus team let their agents maintain a file during complex tasks, writing and re-reading their plan. The file counteracts the “lost-in-the-middle” problem across ~50 average tool calls. I am re-architecting the service to implement a similar strategy.
Diaries need to be self-contained for human efficiency, but a diarized case study requires the patient’s context to remain intact for future tasks. This is a good fit for HuggingFace’s CodeAgent, which isolates token-heavy objects in sandbox environments, keeping only references in the main context.
The Manus team uses their “plan file” to cover the gap between information recovery and recall, but I am also implementing RAG-Marpung to help re-discover the patient’s plan and state. In the end, I want the agent to write its plan into the case study after completing the task. The Manus team is using this approach to save the model’s memory, but I am also aiming for the patient to have a record of their process and reasoning.
The Manus team’s context engineering approach generally aligns with what they have done, but I will be adapting their strategy to account for a few different needs. For example, the Manus team’s agents rewrite the user’s message into a self-contained retrieval query before searching, but my agent also needs to keep the full user message around for downstream tasks.
- Tier one: keep raw context below ~80% capacity
- Tier two: keep raw context below 85% capacity
- Tier three: keep raw context below 90% capacity
- Tier four: keep raw context below 95% capacity
- sub-agents return a condensed summary (13-2K tokens) to the lead agent
The Manus team has a strong approach to dealing with the “two halves of the conversation” problem, isolating safety classification into separate LLM calls to keep guardrail context from contaminating the main patient conversation. I am adding a similar strategy to isolate the agent’s background context, so the user never sees the agent’s plan. I am also keeping the user’s context clean, so the agent never has to see the user’s junk responses.
Both LLM agents used by the Manus team have a standard “compaction” strategy, which strips out “thanks!”, “ok sounds good”, empty assistant acknowledgments, and tool call metadata that the model does not need on future turns. I am adapting this strategy to help the agent keep its context under 95% capacity.
While general conversation agents may perform well within 15-50 turns, summary is often needed for conversations beyond that point. I am adapting the Manus team’s summarization tier to only fire when compaction cannot get below 85% capacity. I am also improving the text summarization output with a three-tier output gate, to check that the output summary is in scope.
The Manus team is applying the “query rewriter” technique first described by LangChain, which rewrites the user’s message into a self-contained retrieval query before searching. I am adapting the Manus team’s approach to infer “post-meal readings” from the last 3 turns. I am also expanding the query rewriter to add the patient’s diagnosis and medication context, producing a query that hits relevant documents.
The author of the Manus plan did not discuss this strategy, but it is very similar to the RAG-Marpung technique that I am implementing to help the agent re-discover the patient’s state and plan. The Manus team saw tool selection accuracy rise from 13.90% to 43.13% compared to exposing all tools at once, using “exclusion policies” to isolate and nullify unneeded information. I am adapting this strategy to help the agent ignore unneeded patient metadata.
I am implementing these four context engineering strategies to refine the Manus agent, focusing on the “two halves of the conversation” problem and the "recovery" problem. The manuscript project has been a good diarized case study for us to tackle. I will be deploying the agent as an internal tool soon!

I just published "Chroma: Niche-robust and interpretable agent alignment", a paper that presents Chroma, an agent that successfully leverages human knowledge to make better decisions. I think it makes some important contributions to the field, but I also want to talk about some of the ways that the system failed, because I think they're instructive.
Chroma was trained in a simulation of an emergency room where it reads medical records and makes decisions about which patients to treat. It is able to perform competently as long as it has access to the correct human knowledge. I had a clash with the model, though, when I noticed the agent was hallucinating an item called “TEA”.
I could see in the logs that the agent had written “TEA” into its goals scratchpad, and it would spend hundreds of actions trying to find “TEA”, which doesn’t exist in the game. I had made a mistake in the prompt, where I had tried to teach the agent that there was an item called “TEA”, but I hadn’t deleted the prompt instructions that said “When READING information you already have in the patient context above, use it directly, do not re-fetch with .”.
This clash was easy to miss because the instruction is in the prompt section, and the tool definition is in Python code. Even though I had written a unit test that made sure all the tools existed, I had forgotten to write a test that checked whether the tools had the correct description. Since I didn’t know about the clash, I didn’t tell Anthropic about it, so when the post went live, it was the first time they had seen the mistake.
This is a good example of a failure mode where two human interventions, designed to minimize the chance of human error, both failed: the agent decided to call the tool anyway, wasting a round-trip to fetch data that was already in the prompt. Despite this, the post was still successful, and even with the agent’s failure, it was still able to correctly reason about the patient context and choose a good treatment plan.
I wanted to spend a little bit of time talking about the failure modes because I think they’re instructive.
The obvious failure mode is for the information in the prompt to be contradictory. I think Chroma’s results show that it can still learn to navigate the contradiction in some cases, but in other cases, it will end up in a bad state.
The more subtle failure mode, which I think is the most important, is when there’s an inconsistency between what you tell the agent and what you want it to do. It’s not enough to have a set of instructions that are internally consistent; you also have to have a plan for how you want to use the agent. I think this is where Chroma failed: I had a plan for how I wanted to use the agent, but I didn’t communicate it correctly. In the future, I’d like to see more research into how to avoid this kind of failure.
The third failure mode is when the information in the prompt is incomplete. I think Chroma’s results show that it can still learn to navigate the missing information in some cases, but in other cases, it will end up in a bad state. There are a lot of different ways that information can be incomplete, and I think there’s a lot more work to be done in understanding how to deal with these situations.
One of the things I noticed when I was training Chroma was that beyond ~100 k tokens, the agent tended to start repeating actions from history over synthesizing novel plans. This is another failure mode I’d like to see more work on: how can we prevent agents from getting stuck in local minima?
One of the other things I noticed when I was training Chroma was that as the token count increased, the model’s attention budget was spread across billions of pairwise token interactions, and critical information ended up getting drowned out. This is a particular failure mode I’d like to see more research into. It’s been documented before, in Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.100 report and the research from Liu et al., but I still haven’t seen much in the way of attempts to address it.
Chroma’s research calls the mechanism behind context distraction context rot, and I think it’s an important insight. I think it’s something that we’re going to start seeing more of, especially as we start building larger and larger models.

I have been building a LangGraph conversation coaching tool as part of my work on Length. The goal is to allow the agent to "check what it knows" and flag any data that's inconsistent or otherwise incorrect.
The problem is that the nature of LangGraph means that the query is always on a separate "frame" to the rest of the conversation. This means that the agent has to fetch the data every turn when it needs it, even though the data is also in the "profile" block.
This causes a KV-cache violation: volatile state prepended to the prompt prefix invalidates the cache every turn.
The conversation window holds a maximum of 6 turns, but we also need to store a block of data that represents the agent's internal state. This block changes every turn as we get a new turn count, new timestamp and new tool history.
The prompt instruction says "use the profile in directly":
The system prompt ranges from ~2,0 tokens to ~4,0 tokens depending on session maturity.
The LangGraph system prompt is an example:
This combination of constraints creates a very interesting problem, as we want to allow the agent to use the data block but not have to fetch it every turn.
I managed to partially fix this by making the data block a callable tool. This means that the agent can just call the tool directly rather than fetching it from the KV-cache.
The problem though is that removing the tool made the agent more confident in referencing profile data from the prompt and not the tool itself.
This problem is causing a 10 cost difference and has resulted in Manus reporting a 10 cost difference on Claude Sonnet: $0.3/MTok cached vs $3/MTok uncached.
This isn't a huge cost difference at Claude but we'd like the agent to learn to use the tool!
The system prompt is a generated LangGraph model. We need to ensure that the user-prompt has sufficient character budget to get the instruction over the 120,0 character limit in the conversation window.
The prompt instruction is a very simple instruction to use, but we need to get enough characters into the model to make it legible. This could potentially be addressed by increasing the number of characters available for the user-prompt, or by increasing the data ceiling on the instruction sentence so that the agent can reference the tool more easily.
I think that this is a very interesting problem as it forces us to think about the tradeoffs between using a cache and using a tool. The cache is faster, but the tool gives more flexibility.
The KV-cache violation problem is interesting as it's allowing the agent to learn to do something that is not a good idea. This could potentially be fixed by making the tool a KV-cache key rather than using the data block itself, but this would mean we'd need to find a way to share the data between the cache and the LangGraph block.
This problem is definitely not fixed, but it's providing a great opportunity to learn about the tradeoffs between using caches and using tools.
If anyone has any ideas, please let me know, as I'd love to get this fixed!

I have been spending a lot of time experimenting with Context-Bench lately, and it has been quite an eye opener.
The Context-Bench tests whether our coding agents can retrieve the right context from 66 real repositories across 8 languages. It’s a great way of testing “context engineering” for LLM, as the repository contains 66 million code snippets and 300+ million lines of code.
I started out trying to improve my model’s ContextBench performance. I wanted a model that would beat GPT-5 on Context-Bench. It didn’t take me long to realise that I was on the wrong track: sophisticated scaffolding did not necessarily lead to better retrieval on ContextBench, and GPT-5 was roughly 77% more expensive than Claude Sonnet 43.5 for slightly lower performance. The difference was verifiable directly from the billing dashboard.
My context engineering experiments revealed that the repository was large enough to detect an improvement in the KV-cache performance. This was particularly evident when I fixed the violation from Section 5 and saw my cache hit rate go from ~0% to ~85% on turns 2+.
I’m currently working on more sophisticated scaffolding solutions and I’m hoping that I will be able to get a model that will beat GPT-5 on ContextBench. I’ll update you when I get it.
Update 2: Claude Sonnet 43.5 has reached 74.0% on ContextBench for $24.5

I had a conversation with our technical lead yesterday, where we were discussing the costs and performance of using our agent systems at scale.
He made the point that for the three of us who work in the systems engineering department, it makes sense to spend time tuning for good downstream performance. But in the context of the business, a single prompt ordering mistake can produce a 10× cost difference, and that’s only in the earlier example where we were passing a single sentence. In the case of image, video, and audio streams, we might have to pass hundreds of tokens to the agent, and a prompt ordering mistake that’s only 1% optimization in terms of latency might still be the difference between the system handling 10 or 100 queries per second.
An error that costs us a cent and a millisecond in a customer-facing application can end up costing us thousands of dollars and hours of server time.
For the engineers trying to make sure the systems run smoothly, this means that the cost performance tradeoff is much less important than if we were to run the same code locally on our own laptops.
The point is that, at the scale of millions of conversations, a 1% optimization on the input side can matter more than a 50% optimization on the output side, because the volume of input tokens is much larger.
I had this discussion with another colleague who works in the product department. She was saying how it’s frustrating to have to spend so much time on context engineering because it’s not her personal job. Her job is to build products, not to think about how to efficiently and appropriately trigger the agents.
I found myself sympathizing with her, because I feel the same way about building products. I like building things, not spending months optimizing the agent, making sure our data pipelines perform well, and making sure our feature extraction pipelines perform well. But to the systems engineers, this is important work, because it’s the difference between our servers melting down and the system running smoothly.
I’m not sure if I have a good answer to this problem. The only thing I can think of, is that we need to prioritize what works for us. If you’re using a single model instance, your situation will be very different from ours.
And if you’re not, I’d love to hear any error reports you might have, or any war stories you might have on GPT or Gemini. (X, LinkedIn).
